631.title: Come, Lord Jesus (Apocalypse 22:17–21)
631.carry: take the water of life, freely
631.howItsDone: Catholics voice this longing at every Mass, in the prayer after the Lord's Prayer that speaks of waiting for the coming of the Savior, and especially in Advent, the season of preparing for Christ's coming; some pray maranatha as a short, repeated prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tabernacle: the city coming down, and every tear wiped away. Your line was behold, I make all things new.

Back on day three hundred thirty-two, a library opened at its first page: in the beginning. Since then, kings, prophets, psalms, Gospels, letters and visions. Today, the last page. And the Bible doesn't end with a summary, or a moral, or a final warning. It ends with a conversation. Someone says come. Someone answers I'm coming. And then the last prayer in the whole book, three words long. An older form of it turns up in one of Paul's letters, in another language.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE OF THE LIBRARY.` → `NOT A SUMMARY: A CONVERSATION.` → `THE BIBLE'S LAST PRAYER.`

segments.voice: First, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the spirit and the bride say: Come. And he that heareth, let him say: Come." The Spirit and the bride, the Church, call out to Christ. Then the invitation turns toward anyone listening: let him that thirsts come, and take the water of life, freely. Come goes both ways. Then Christ answers: "Surely I come quickly: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." That's the Bible's last prayer. Now back to Paul. Writing in Greek to the Corinthians, he leaves one Aramaic word untranslated: maranatha. Aramaic was the language of Jesus and his first followers in Galilee. Paul keeps the word the way you'd keep a word from a grandmother's language, because no other word feels right. Scholars discuss two readings: maran atha, our Lord has come; or marana tha, our Lord, come! Christians can pray both. He has come; come again. An early Christian handbook called the Didache puts maranatha in its prayers after the Eucharist, and come, Lord Jesus sounds, to some scholars, like that same old prayer put into Greek. Then the Bible ends with a blessing: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." Catholics pray this longing at every Mass: after the Lord's Prayer, the priest prays for the people as they wait in hope for the coming of our Savior. And all through Advent, the Church sings come. The book whose first page has God saying let there be light ends with his people saying come.
screen: `THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY: COME.` · `SURELY I COME QUICKLY.` · `MARANATHA: OUR LORD, COME.` · `PRAYED AT EVERY MASS AND IN ADVENT.` · then, large: `AMEN. COME, LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: Think of what in your life, or in the world, most needs to be made new, a sorrow, an illness, a war, a relationship, and hold it gently. If you pray, say the Bible's last prayer on each out-breath, come, Lord Jesus, or the old Aramaic word, maranatha, until it's almost a whisper. If you don't, just feel what it's like to long for something to come.
Maranatha. Aramaic, from the first Christians: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. The Bible's last prayer. Today's word.

Your line: take the water of life, freely. And that's the Apocalypse: an unveiling, the first and the last, first charity, not lukewarm, the knock, holy, the Lamb, every tongue, the woman, Babylon, the supper, tabernacle, and maranatha. The last page, turned.

632.title: How the calendar works
632.hook: solemnities, feasts and memorials, with Sundays at the center
632.howItsDone: Catholics follow the General Roman Calendar, which ranks each day as a solemnity, feast, memorial or weekday; parish calendars, missals and liturgy apps show each day's rank and color.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last page of the Bible: maranatha, and take the water of life, freely. The book, read in order, is done.

Open a parish wall calendar and the squares are not all equal. Some days are printed in red. Some have a saint's name in small type. Some just say Tuesday of the twenty-third week. A few say something stronger, and the whole parish knows it: Christmas, Easter, the Assumption. The Bible has been read cover to cover; now comes the way the Church hears it, one feast at a time, around a year with its own shape. First, a key.
screen: `NOT EVERY SQUARE IS EQUAL.` → `FROM THE BOOK TO THE YEAR.` → `A KEY TO THE MAP.`

segments.voice: The Church's calendar sorts its days into ranks. At the top is a solemnity, from the Latin sollemnitas, a yearly, festive observance: Christmas, Easter, Pentecost, the Immaculate Conception, Saints Peter and Paul. A solemnity begins the evening before, the way a Jewish sabbath begins at sunset, and at Mass the Gloria is sung and the Creed is said. One step down is a feast: an apostle, the Holy Family, the Conversion of Saint Paul. A feast keeps to its own day, with the Gloria and usually without the Creed. Below that comes a memorial, a saint remembered, some obligatory, some optional. And under them all, the plain weekday, which the books call a feria. Here's the surprise: Sunday sits at the center. The Second Vatican Council called the Lord's Day the original feast day, kept every week in memory of the resurrection. An ordinary Sunday outranks almost every saint. The Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter outrank even most solemnities: when one collides with them, the solemnity moves. An official table, a ladder of thirteen steps, settles every collision. It sounds like bookkeeping, but the effect is that the year breathes: long green stretches of ordinary weeks, then the purple seasons of waiting, then white and gold for the great days. A psalm the Church sings at Easter says it plainly: "This is the day which the Lord hath made: let us be glad and rejoice therein." The calendar says which joy today is. And the year doesn't start in January. It starts tomorrow, with Advent.

segments.voice: If you have a missal, a parish calendar or a liturgy app, look up today: a solemnity, a feast, a memorial or a plain weekday, a saint named or not, and what color the priest is wearing. If you can't look it up, just guess. A plain weekday is not a lesser day, since most of life is lived on them; if you pray, greet today by its name, and if not, just notice that it has one.

633.title: First Sunday of Advent (Mark 13:33–37)
633.hook: the new year starts with watch
633.howItsDone: On the First Sunday of Advent, Catholic churches begin the new liturgical year in violet vestments, and many parishes and families light the first candle of an Advent wreath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the key to the calendar: solemnity at the top, and Sunday at the center. Your line was every day has a rank.

New Year's Eve has a countdown and a party. The Church's new year begins on a Sunday in late November or early December, in purple, with a single candle and a warning. No fireworks. The first gospel of the year isn't a birth story. It's a house at night, a master who has gone away, and a doorkeeper told to stay awake. In the year when Mark's Gospel is read on Sundays, these five verses, Mark 13:33 to 37, open everything. And the year's first word is a command.
screen: `A NEW YEAR IN PURPLE.` → `A HOUSE AT NIGHT.` → `THE FIRST WORD IS A COMMAND.`

segments.voice: Advent comes from the Latin adventus, a coming or an arrival. Across the Sundays before Christmas, the Church looks two ways at once: back to the first coming, the birth in Bethlehem, and forward to the coming at the end of time. The first Sunday leans hard forward. In Mark, Jesus tells a small story. A man goes on a long journey. He leaves his house in his servants' hands, gives each one a job, and tells the porter at the door to keep watch. Nobody knows when he'll be back: in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or in the morning. Four times, named one after another, so every hour of the dark is covered. Don't let him come suddenly and find you sleeping. Then the last line, which Mark aims past the disciples at every reader: "And what I say to you, I say to all: Watch." The Greek word is grēgoreite, stay awake, keep alert, a word for staying up when sleep would be easier. Notice what it doesn't say: panic, or calculate the date, or stare at the sky. Each servant has work. Watching, in this story, looks like doing your job well while staying awake to who might walk through the door. That's why the Church starts its year here. Before the manger, before the shepherds and the star, the first thing asked is attention. And on this Sunday, in some homes, someone lights the first of four candles on a wreath: one small flame against the dark.
screen: `ADVENT: A COMING.` · `THE MASTER GOES AWAY.` · `FOUR WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.` · `WATCHING LOOKS LIKE WORK.` · then, large: `WHAT I SAY TO YOU, I SAY TO ALL: WATCH.`

segments.voice: If you have an Advent wreath, light the first candle; if not, any candle, or a single lamp in a dark room, will do. Watch the flame the way a doorkeeper watches a door, awake, unhurried, ready, and when your mind wanders, come back to the light. If you pray, you can say the word Advent keeps singing, come; if not, just keep watch with the flame.
Gregoreite, stay awake. Mark thirteen: the Church's new year begins with a house at night and a porter told to keep watch. Today's word.
Your line: watch. The Church's new year opens with a single, wide-awake word. See you tomorrow.

634.title: Advent with Isaiah
634.hook: Advent's first readings come mostly from Isaiah: a people that walked in darkness
634.howItsDone: Through Advent, the first reading at Mass is very often from Isaiah, and Isaiah 9 is read at the Mass during the night of Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gregoreite: a house at night, and a porter told to stay awake. Your line was one word, watch.

Sit in a pew on a weekday in early Advent and listen to the first reading. Day after day it opens the same way: a reading from the book of the prophet Isaiah. Swords beaten into plowshares. A wolf lying down with a lamb. A shoot from a stump. The desert blooming. Isaiah is the voice the Church hands Advent, so much that some people call him the Advent prophet. And the Isaiah line the Church saves for Christmas night is about people in the dark.
screen: `A READING FROM ISAIAH.` → `PLOWSHARES, WOLF, SHOOT.` → `PEOPLE IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Isaiah preached in Jerusalem in the days of King Ahaz and King Hezekiah. His world was frightening: Assyria, the great power of the day, was swallowing the small kingdoms around Judah, and Isaiah names the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up by the Sea of Galilee, as the ones brought low. Into that darkness he speaks in the past tense, as if the rescue had already happened. The Douay-Rheims reads: "The people that walked in darkness, have seen a great light." Light is risen, he says, on those in the region of the shadow of death. Then a child: a son is given, the government will rest on his shoulder, and his names pile up, ending with Prince of Peace. Jewish readers place this in Isaiah's own time, and some Jewish commentators have understood the child as a king of Judah, Hezekiah. Christians read it as well as a promise fulfilled in Jesus, and Matthew's Gospel quotes the darkness-and-light line when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the very region Isaiah named. Both readings live with the same words. Why give Isaiah to Advent? Because Advent is about waiting in the dark without pretending it's already bright. Isaiah never says the darkness is small. He says a light shows up inside it. And Catholics hear this passage at the Mass during the night of Christmas, so Advent's prophet gets the first word of Christmas too. In early December the northern nights keep getting longer, and the readings answer with one stubborn sentence.
screen: `ASSYRIA AND THE DARK NORTH.` · `A GREAT LIGHT, IN THE PAST TENSE.` · `A CHILD, A SON, A PRINCE OF PEACE.` · `SAVED FOR CHRISTMAS NIGHT.` · then, large: `THE PEOPLE THAT WALKED IN DARKNESS.`

If you pray, hold that place up in the light; if not, simply keep both in view.

635.title: The Immaculate Conception (8 December)
635.hook: readings from Genesis 3 and the Annunciation
635.carry: full of grace from the start
635.howItsDone: Catholics keep December 8 as a solemnity, a holy day of obligation in many countries, with readings from Genesis 3 and Luke's account of the Annunciation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hezekiah, and a line for the long nights: a great light.

Ask a room of people what the Immaculate Conception is, and someone will probably say: it's when Jesus was conceived without a human father. It's an easy mix-up. But that's the virgin birth, a different teaching. December 8 is about Mary herself, and the first moment of her own life. In the middle of Advent, nine months before her birthday on September 8, the Church stops for a solemnity. And the readings it chooses go all the way back to a garden.
screen: `NOT THE VIRGIN BIRTH.` → `MARY'S OWN BEGINNING.` → `BACK TO A GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The first reading is Genesis 3. Adam and Eve have eaten the fruit and hidden. God walks in the garden and calls, where art thou? Then God speaks to the serpent, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head." She, in that translation, because the Latin Vulgate says ipsa; the Hebrew points instead to the woman's offspring, he or it. Either way, Catholic tradition hears a first promise here: a woman and her child, and a struggle with evil that ends in victory. Then the gospel jumps to Nazareth. The angel Gabriel greets a young woman: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." Full of grace translates one Greek word, kecharitōmenē, a form that suggests favor already given and still lasting. In 1854, Pope Pius IX defined what Catholics had long celebrated: that Mary, from the first instant of her conception, was kept free of original sin, by a singular grace, in view of what her son would do. Not because she earned it, and not apart from Christ, but as the first fruit of his work. Side by side, the two readings show a shape: Eve, who reached for the fruit in the garden, and Mary, who would say be it done to me, in Nazareth. Christian traditions differ here. Orthodox Christians honor Mary as all-holy but generally don't accept the teaching in this defined form, and Protestant churches generally don't teach it. For Catholics it's a holy day, and in the United States, Mary under this title is the nation's patroness.
screen: `GENESIS 3: SHE SHALL CRUSH.` · `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.` · `1854: FREE FROM THE FIRST INSTANT.` · `EVE IN THE GARDEN, MARY IN NAZARETH.` · then, large: `FULL OF GRACE FROM THE START.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say one Hail Mary slowly, aloud or silently; it opens with the angel's greeting and then Elizabeth's before it asks anything, so let each phrase land. If you don't pray, sit with the greeting itself, full of grace, and think of a beginning in your own life that was a gift, something you didn't earn. Then rest in the quiet.

636.title: Our Lady of Guadalupe (12 December)
636.hook: the patroness of the Americas; roses in December
636.howItsDone: On December 12 many Catholics, especially Mexican and Mexican-American communities, gather before dawn to sing Las Mañanitas to Our Lady of Guadalupe and bring roses to her image.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kecharitomene: not the virgin birth, but Mary herself, full of grace from the start.

Before dawn on December 12, in Mexico City and in parishes from Los Angeles to Chicago, people gather outside churches to sing Las Mañanitas, the birthday song, to Mary. Mariachis in the dark. Roses everywhere, before a framed image of a young woman with her head bowed, dressed in a starred mantle, standing on a crescent moon. Her basilica in Mexico City stands at the foot of a hill. The story behind all those roses begins with a poor man on that hill in winter.
screen: `SINGING IN THE DARK.` → `ROSES EVERYWHERE.` → `A MAN ON A HILL.`

segments.voice: December 1531, in the years just after the Spanish conquest of the Aztec capital. Juan Diego, an Indigenous man and a recent convert, is walking past the hill of Tepeyac. He hears birdsong, then a voice calling him by name. A young woman, speaking his own language, Nahuatl, tells him she is the Mother of the true God and asks for a church to be built there. He goes to the bishop, Juan de Zumárraga, who is unconvinced and asks for a sign. Then Juan Diego's uncle falls gravely ill, and Juan Diego, embarrassed, takes a different path around the hill to fetch a priest and avoid her. She meets him anyway. The best-known account gives her words, in paraphrase: do not be afraid; am I not here, I who am your mother? She tells him his uncle is already healed and sends him up the hill, where in the cold of December he finds roses blooming. He gathers them into his tilma, his rough cloak, and carries them to the bishop. When he opens it, the roses fall, and on the cloth is the image people still visit today. The fullest account, the Nican Mopohua, was published in Nahuatl in 1649, and historians debate how early the story was written down; the Church's devotion rests on long tradition and on the image itself. In 2002, Pope John Paul II canonized Juan Diego, and popes have named Mary under this title patroness of the Americas. In the story, notice who she chooses: not the bishop, but a conquered man, addressed in his own tongue, by name.
screen: `TEPEYAC, DECEMBER 1531.` · `THE BISHOP ASKS FOR A SIGN.` · `AM I NOT HERE?` · `ROSES IN THE TILMA.` · then, large: `I WHO AM YOUR MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Picture a church near you, its door, and the place by an image of Mary where people leave roses; if you can go today, you might bring one flower. For now, think of someone who has said to you, in their own way, I'm here: a parent, a friend, a stranger in a hard hour. If you pray, offer that person to Our Lady; if not, simply give thanks for them.
Nican Mopohua, 'here it is told.' The Nahuatl account of Mary's appearance to Juan Diego at Tepeyac in 1531, published in 1649. Today's word.

637.title: Gaudete Sunday (Philippians 4:4)
637.hook: the rose candle: rejoice, the Lord is near
637.howItsDone: On the third Sunday of Advent many Catholic parishes light the rose candle of the Advent wreath, and the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nican Mopohua: roses in December, and a question that's also a promise, am I not here.

Look at an Advent wreath in its third week. Two purple candles have burned down a little. Then there's one that isn't purple at all. It's pink, or as the Church calls it, rose. On the third Sunday of Advent the priest may wear rose vestments too, a color that appears only twice a year. People who don't know why sometimes think the florist got the order wrong. The real reason is one Latin word, the first word sung at that Sunday's Mass for many centuries.
screen: `TWO PURPLE, THEN ONE ROSE.` → `ONLY TWICE A YEAR.` → `ONE LATIN WORD.`

segments.voice: Gaudete means rejoice, said to more than one person. It opens the entrance chant of the third Sunday of Advent, taken from Paul's letter to the Philippians. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice." The reason follows a verse later: "The Lord is nigh." Here's what gives it weight. Paul wrote this letter in chains. He mentions his bonds again and again, and he isn't sure he'll leave prison alive. So this isn't a cheerful man telling everyone to smile. It's a prisoner insisting that joy has a source outside his circumstances. Advent is a season of waiting, and waiting can turn grim. So halfway through, the Church lightens the color. Purple softens to rose, like the first light of dawn at the edge of the sky. It isn't Christmas yet; the waiting isn't over. But the nearness has started to show. Gaudete Sunday ends a week that has walked a long way. It opened with the Bible's last prayer, maranatha, take the water of life, freely. Then, every day has a rank. The new year began with one word, watch. Isaiah gave a great light. Kecharitomene gave full of grace from the start. Guadalupe gave am I not here. And now rose, and rejoice. Read in a row, they make a small Advent of their own: a cry, a calendar, a lookout, a light, a girl, a mother, and joy on the way.
screen: `GAUDETE: REJOICE, ALL OF YOU.` · `WRITTEN IN CHAINS.` · `PURPLE SOFTENS TO ROSE.` · `A WEEK OF ADVENT, LOOKED BACK.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS NIGH.`

segments.voice: If you can, put on one bright thing before you sit, a scarf, socks, a ring, the pink shirt you never wear, and sit with it on. Name one honest reason for joy today, even small, even beside something hard, the way Paul found his in chains, without forcing a feeling. If you pray, say Paul's words, rejoice in the Lord always; if not, let the color remind you.
Gaudete. Latin for rejoice, said to many. It names the third Sunday of Advent, with its rose candle and rose vestments. Today's word.
Your line: rejoice. Joy can come even in chains, because the Lord is nigh. See you tomorrow.
